title: Checkpoint: First Peoples, New Worlds
objective: After this level you can explain what North America was like before 1600 and how the arrival of Europeans changed it.
summary: Europeans entered a crowded continent: nations, cities and confederacies were already here. A timeline from Cahokia to the Pueblo Revolt ties the chapter together.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: Europeans didn’t find an empty continent, but a crowded one.
cards.body: Hundreds of languages, cities, farms and confederacies were already here. Let’s put the whole chapter on one timeline.

events.label: Cliff dwellings rise at Mesa Verde
Columbus’s voyage begins the Columbian Exchange
The Pueblo Revolt drives out the Spanish

cards.headline: Newcomers in someone else’s country
cards.body: St. Augustine is 42 years older than Jamestown, and both were built in lands that already had rulers. In Virginia, Powhatan’s chiefdom united dozens of tribes. In the Northeast, five nations governed themselves under the Great Law of Peace. In New Mexico, the Pueblos could rise together and drive Spain out. What the newcomers carried mattered as much as who they were: across the Americas, populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650, largely because of epidemics. The map was never blank. It was being redrawn.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: How North America was a continent of nations before 1492, and how Europe’s arrival changed it.
What Cahokia, Chaco and Mesa Verde reveal about the towns built before Europeans came.
Why epidemics devastated Native peoples while crops and horses crossed the Atlantic.
How Spain and England entered lands already ruled by the Pueblos and Powhatan.

questions.prompt: First Peoples, New Worlds: which order of events is right?

options.label: Cahokia flourishes, St. Augustine is founded, the Pueblo Revolt
St. Augustine is founded, Cahokia flourishes, the Pueblo Revolt
Cahokia flourishes, the Pueblo Revolt, St. Augustine is founded
The Pueblo Revolt, Cahokia flourishes, St. Augustine is founded

questions.explanation: Cahokia flourished from about 950 to 1350; St. Augustine was founded in 1565; the Pueblo Revolt came in 1680.

questions.prompt: The find that convinced archaeologists that people reached the Americas before the Clovis culture was _____.

options.label: the Jamestown fort in Virginia
Monks Mound at Cahokia
options.rationale: It’s about a thousand years old, far younger than Clovis.

options.label: the Monte Verde site in Chile
the Hiawatha Belt

questions.explanation: Monte Verde, over 14,000 years old, was broadly accepted as pre-Clovis in 1997.

questions.prompt: Why is “an empty continent” a poor description of North America around 1600?

options.label: Europeans had settled most of it by then
It held many nations with their own leaders
The Ice Age had not yet ended there
Its peoples all spoke a single language

questions.explanation: Hundreds of languages and nations, like Powhatan’s chiefdom and the Haudenosaunee, were already there.

questions.prompt: Under the Great Law of Peace, how did the Haudenosaunee council make decisions?

options.label: The largest nation decided alone
A simple majority of chiefs
Each nation had one vote, and decisions were unanimous
A single elected king decided

questions.explanation: Each nation had one vote, and decisions had to be unanimous.

questions.prompt: Cahokia and Mesa Verde both emptied out before Europeans arrived. What likely factor did they share?

options.label: Attacks by Spanish soldiers
Epidemics brought from Europe
The Tuscarora conquest
options.rationale: The Tuscarora lived far away and later.

options.label: Environmental stress, from drought or damaged land

questions.explanation: Cahokia likely suffered from environmental damage; Mesa Verde from the Great Drought of 1276 to 1299.
